questions.q: According to this lesson, why is it misleading to think of bias as something a model 'has,' like a single bug?
options: Bias only ever comes from one single source: the training data
Bias can enter at several different points — training data, labeling, and deployment context — so fixing one doesn't fix the others
Bias is impossible to detect in any AI system
Only models trained before 2020 can exhibit bias
questions.explain: The lesson identifies training data bias, labeling bias, and deployment context bias as separate entry points, meaning a fix at one stage doesn't address the others.

questions.q: What is 'deployment context bias,' as defined in this lesson?
options: A bug that only appears when a model is deployed on a specific cloud provider
A model performing evenly in testing but producing unequal outcomes once used in a narrower real-world context the test set didn't represent
A type of bias that only affects image-generation models
The cost difference between deploying a model on different hardware
questions.explain: A model can test evenly overall yet still produce unequal outcomes once applied in a specific real-world context not well represented in testing.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the paired-prompt test described in this lesson (e.g., swapping only a name between two otherwise identical prompts)?
options: To formally prove, with statistical certainty, that a system is completely unbiased
To replace the need for any further bias testing permanently
To provide a cheap, fast way to surface an obvious problem before investing in heavier red-teaming and eval-dataset work
To measure a model's latency and cost under different prompts
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that a handful of paired prompts can't prove a system is unbiased — it's a quick first check, not a rigorous statistical test.

questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish between a model's 'behavior' and the 'outcome' of using it?
options: Behavior and outcome always mean exactly the same thing
Behavior asks whether similar inputs are treated similarly; outcome asks whether results actually land evenly across groups once deployed — a model can pass one and fail the other
Only outcome matters; model behavior is irrelevant to fairness
Behavior can only be measured after a model is retired
questions.explain: A model can treat individual prompts consistently and still produce an unequal overall outcome depending on how and by whom it's actually used.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say there isn't one universal technical definition of 'fair'?
options: Fairness has never been studied in traditional machine learning
Competing technical definitions of fairness (like equal selection rates vs. equal error rates) can conflict, so satisfying one can mean violating another on the same dataset
Fairness is purely a legal term with no technical meaning at all
Every fairness definition always agrees with every other one on any dataset
questions.explain: Different fairness definitions can be mutually incompatible on the same data, so the practical step is being explicit about which definition a system is held to.
